catalog_quote: The Kman tone system has three phonetic tone heights marked as follows; High- ˊ Mid ˉ Low ˋ A macron (ˉ) over a vowel represents mid-tone and not length throughout this grammar. However, of these, only the mid-tone occurs on monosyllabic roots in isolation. However, strikingly, a three-way contrast on monosyllabic roots can be heard in sentence context, since the tone on the verb root may be any of the three heights in context. ... The underlying system consists of glide tones which can apply either to single segments but form a system of suprasegmental patterns applied to polysyllabic words and compounds. The glides so far identified are High-Mid, High-Low and Mid-Low ... Kman is a sesquisyllabic language of a type common in the SE Asian region. new_statements.quote: 2.3 Tones. Like most regional languages, Kman is tonal, but the tone-system is relatively simple. There are two level tones, High (ˊ) and Low (ˋ), a rising (ˇ) and a rare falling (ˆ) tone. Glide tones also arise from VV sequences. [...] Examples of three-way contrast are quite rare on single syllable words. [p. 3] || 3.3 Tone. Is it necessary to write tone? Tone is marked throughout this working paper, but there are relatively few minimal pairs which can be confused by not marking the tone. [p. 9] || (2018 booklet, p. 58:) Kman has three levels of tone, as well as glide tones, i.e. tones that slide between two levels. [...] There seem to be no words which have a high tone in isolation.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (catalog-all-2026-09-12, from Blench & Kri 2019 grammar sect. 2.3) records Kman as tonal-OR-pitch accent with no word-stress statement and an empty rule. The 2015 proposal is the same author's earlier sketch: same type (lexical tone, no stress statement anywhere). The only difference is in the tone inventory (2015: two levels H/L + rising + rare falling; 2018 booklet and 2019 grammar: three heights H/M/L + glides), an earlier analysis later revised by the author himself; it does not bear on stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kman is described as a tonal language (2015 analysis: two level tones High/Low plus rising and rare falling contour tones, glides also from VV sequences; the 2018 booklet revises this to three tone levels plus glide tones). The phonology section (2. Phonology: consonants, vowels, tones) contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence; a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for stress/accent/prominen/intonation/pitch/emphasis gives 0 hits in both the 2015 proposal and the 2018 booklet.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress rule stated). Tone-related remarks only: words consisting entirely of consonants 'sometimes' carry a floating tone, elsewhere tone appears neutralised (pp. 3-4); tone may be left unmarked in the orthography (p. 9).
new_statements.identity_note: All three Blench documents describe Kman (= Miju Mishmi = Geman/Kaman) as spoken around Tezu, Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh; no sub-dialect is singled out. (The Sastry 1984 Mishmi Grammar logged in the earlier reading is on the Digaru/Taraon dialect, a different language, and is not part of this retry.)

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation and locator check out verbatim in the held Blench & Kri 2019 PDF/txt (sect. 2.3.1 pp. 25-26; 2.3.5 p. 29), and the record's negative claim (no occurrence of 'stress'/'accent') is confirmed by a full-text search for stress/accent over the full text. (2) The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule stated' rests on a 2019 fieldwork grammar draft by the principal current researcher on Kman with a native-speaker co-author; it is the best English-language source and the latest description overall. The only fuller works are Chinese-language grammars of the Zayü (Geman) variety (Li Daqin 2002, 324 pp; Li Daqin 2019), which Blench read and criticises on tone; nothing seen suggests they would overturn a 'tonal' coding, though they might add a weak-presyllable statement that refines the domain note. sources.citation: Sastry, G. Devi Prasada (1985). Mishmi Grammar. Central Institute of Indian Languages.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The description is of the Digaru dialect (= Taraon / Digaro-Mishmi, Glottolog diga1241), stated explicitly on p. 5; Miju (Kman) data were used only for 'verification and cross-checking' and no Miju-specific phonological statement is made. The author treats Idu, Digaru and Miju as dialects of one 'Mishmi' language, whereas Glottolog lists them as separate languages, so the tonal description cannot be credited to Kman. Relative to the catalog (Kman listed with an empty rule, no existing statements) the work is silent on Kman stress; it neither agrees nor contradicts.
